subject: Architecture
title: The Walkie Talkie: London's Death Ray
description: A quick, practical guide to The Walkie Talkie: London's Death Ray.

hook.text: A London skyscraper melted a Jaguar car parked across the street — its curved glass focused sunlight like a lens.

buildup.text: 20 Fenchurch Street — nicknamed the 'Walkie Talkie' — has a concave south-facing glass facade.

discovery.text: The curved surface concentrated solar radiation into a beam, reaching temperatures over 200°F on the street below.

twist.text: A reporter fried an egg on the sidewalk using only the reflected sunlight. The story went viral worldwide.

climax.text: Engineers installed a permanent sunshade — a horizontal brise-soleil — to block the dangerous reflections.

punchline.text: A building that cooks cars. Architecture's most embarrassing physics lesson.

quiz.question: What caused the 'death ray' effect at 20 Fenchurch Street?
options: Reflective cladding panels redirected sunlight at street level
The concave glass facade focused sunlight like a lens
Heat exhaust from the HVAC system overheated the sidewalk

details.summary: 20 Fenchurch Street in London, nicknamed the Walkie Talkie, made headlines in 2013 when its concave glass facade focused sunlight into a beam hot enough to melt car parts and scorch storefronts. The building's shape acted as a parabolic mirror, concentrating solar energy at street level.
details.whyItMatters: The Walkie Talkie incident showed that modern building facades can have dangerous unintended consequences. It forced architects and engineers to take solar reflection seriously as a design constraint.
takeaways: The Walkie Talkie's concave facade focused sunlight into a death ray
Concentrated solar energy melted car parts and scorched shops below
The incident changed how architects model solar reflection

faq.question: How did the Walkie Talkie create a death ray?
faq.answer: The building's concave south-facing glass facade acted like a parabolic mirror, concentrating reflected sunlight into a focused beam at street level. Temperatures at the focal point reportedly reached 117°C (243°F), enough to melt plastic car trim and ignite doorway carpets.

faq.question: How was the problem fixed?
faq.answer: Developers installed a permanent horizontal brise-soleil (sun shade) across the facade to break up and scatter the reflected light before it could concentrate. The fix was effective but altered the building's appearance and added millions in unplanned construction costs.
